power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Anxiety decreased over the programme as a whole: the pooled within-arm change in STAI-6 from week 1 to week 4 was -5.72 points (95% HDI, -9.35 to -2.00; posterior probability of exceeding the MCID, 0.93; d = -0.40; per-arm estimates in S8.13). Medical hypnosis did not differ from structured relaxation on week-4 STAI-6: adjusted mean difference, +0.95 (95% HDI, -5.85 to 7.42; standardised effect size d = 0.07), with a posterior probability of hypnosis advantage of 0.38 and of exceeding the 3-point MCID of 0.12 (Table 2). At the realised sample (intracluster correlation 0.127, design effect 1.29), the minimal detectable between-arm effect at 80% power for the primary analysis was approximately 7.5 STAI-6 points (S12); the posterior is more informative than this threshold, placing 0.62 of its mass on a clinically negligible between-arm difference and at most 0.06 on an advantage of two MCIDs or more in either direction. The registered trajectory model likewise converged to a null week-4 contrast (-1.08; 95% HDI, -7.54 to 5.47; P[hypnosis < relaxation] = 0.63); both estimates lie within the MCID.

The sample size was derived by simulation for a mixed-effects model with cluster random intercepts (13): 10 clusters of five participants per arm (n=100) gave 83% power (95% confidence interval, 80-86%) at a two-sided α of 0.05 to detect a 10% (approximately 4.7-point) additional STAI-6 reduction with hypnosis, assuming a 24% reduction with hypnosis, as in HYPNOBPCO_1 (9), and 14% with relaxation from a baseline of 47 points. The target was set at 120 to allow for 20% attrition. Given the novelty of the approach, no empirical pre-existing intracluster correlation coefficient was available at simulation time.

text.text: In a cluster-randomised trial in COPD pulmonary rehabilitation, medical hypnosis did not reduce anxiety more than matched relaxation.
An exploratory analysis suggests greater hypnosis benefit in patients with predominantly sensory dyspnoea burden.
Helebor Foundation, France.
The funders had no role in the design or conduct of the trial, data analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, or the decision to submit.
The views expressed are those of the authors.

Anxiety is among the most prevalent and least adequately managed comorbidities of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), affecting 22% to 56% of patients across populations and disease stages (1) (2) (3) (4) (5).
text.formatted: Anxiety is among the most prevalent and least adequately managed comorbidities of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), affecting 22% to 56% of patients across populations and disease stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: It is associated with worse dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance, greater health care utilisation, and higher risks of 30-day readmission, exacerbation, and death, independent of disease severity (1, 2).
text.formatted: It is associated with worse dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance, greater health care utilisation, and higher risks of 30-day readmission, exacerbation, and death, independent of disease severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: Pharmacological management of dyspnoea-associated anxiety in COPD has shown mixed efficacy (3).
text.formatted: Pharmacological management of dyspnoea-associated anxiety in COPD has shown mixed efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: The 2026 Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease strategy recommends combining pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) with cognitive-behavioural therapy and mind-body interventions (e.g., mindfulness-based therapy, yoga, relaxation) to alleviate anxiety and depressive symptoms (3, 4).
text.formatted: The 2026 Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease strategy recommends combining pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) with cognitive-behavioural therapy and mind-body interventions (e.g., mindfulness-based therapy, yoga, relaxation) to alleviate anxiety and depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: However, the benefit of these interventions is heterogeneous, with a substantial subset of patients deriving limited improvement (5), calling for a better understanding of what determines intervention success.
text.formatted: However, the benefit of these interventions is heterogeneous, with a substantial subset of patients deriving limited improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>, calling for a better understanding of what determines intervention success.

text.text: Mind-body adjuncts to PR are increasingly studied, but the evidence base is limited by comparator choice.

Most trials of cognitive-behavioural therapy (6), mindfulness-based interventions (7), and hypnosis (8) in COPD have used waitlist or treatment-as-usual comparators that conflate intervention-specific effects with the nonspecific benefits of any structured psychological contact embedded in PR.
text.formatted: Most trials of cognitive-behavioural therapy (6), mindfulness-based interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>, and hypnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> in COPD have used waitlist or treatment-as-usual comparators that conflate intervention-specific effects with the nonspecific benefits of any structured psychological contact embedded in PR.

text.text: The present trial addresses this gap with an active comparator matched on these nonspecific components, with a preregistered multi-instrument approach to measure anxiety across multiple clinically relevant constructs (STAI-6, MDP, HADS-A).
The trial focuses on medical hypnosis, based on the strength of two precedents (9, 10).
text.formatted: The trial focuses on medical hypnosis, based on the strength of two precedents <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: First, a single 15-minute session of medical hypnosis delivered to inpatients with severe COPD produced an immediate and clinically meaningful reduction in state anxiety (9), establishing proof of concept in this population.
text.formatted: First, a single 15-minute session of medical hypnosis delivered to inpatients with severe COPD produced an immediate and clinically meaningful reduction in state anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>, establishing proof of concept in this population.

text.text: Second, mechanistic work in healthy volunteers under inspiratory threshold loading and hypercapnia with restrained ventilation showed that hypnosis attenuates both the sensory and affective dimensions of experimental dyspnoea through combined effects on breathing drive and cortical engagement (10).
text.formatted: Second, mechanistic work in healthy volunteers under inspiratory threshold loading and hypercapnia with restrained ventilation showed that hypnosis attenuates both the sensory and affective dimensions of experimental dyspnoea through combined effects on breathing drive and cortical engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that hypnosis acts on both anxiety and dyspnoea perception and may be a viable low-cost adjunct for anxiety management in COPD.
Whether this anxiolytic response is reliable in clinical practice, and whether it is uniform across patients or different expressions of dyspnoea, remained unanswered.

In this trial, we evaluated the efficacy of medical hypnosis as an adjunct to inpatient PR for anxiety in COPD, using structured relaxation as an active comparator matched on session length, structure, practitioner pool, and self-management framing.
By holding these nonspecific components constant, we aimed to isolate the cognitive-control components more specific to hypnosis, namely sensory suggestion and interoceptive redirection (11, 12).
text.formatted: By holding these nonspecific components constant, we aimed to isolate the cognitive-control components more specific to hypnosis, namely sensory suggestion and interoceptive redirection <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12)</ref>.

text.text: We hypothesised that both arms would reduce anxiety and, as the trial's confirmatory objective, that adjunctive hypnosis would reduce anxiety more than structured relaxation.
Separately, in an exploratory post hoc moderator analysis, we examined whether the hypnotic advantage varied with baseline sensory and affective dyspnoea burden.
All patients admitted to PR between September 27, 2021, and January 31, 2024, were screened consecutively.

Eligible participants were adults older than 30 years with COPD confirmed by spirometry (forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity <0.70), a modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea grade of 2 or higher, and at least 10 pack-years of tobacco exposure.
text.formatted: Eligible participants were adults older than 30 years with COPD confirmed by spirometry (forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity <0.70), a modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea grade of 2 or higher, and at least 10 pack-years of tobacco exposure.

text.text: Exclusion criteria (supplementary material, S2.2) included pregnancy, severe cardiac insufficiency or pulmonary arterial hypertension, active malignancy, hypercapnic encephalopathy, deafness, anaemia, psychotic illness, and clinically significant cognitive impairment.
Sex was recorded as sex assigned at birth.
The unit of randomisation was the consecutive PR cohort (cluster).
Patients were assigned to cohorts on clinical grounds, and each cohort was constituted before it was randomised, so neither allocation nor its foreknowledge could influence cohort composition.

Allocation was paired at the cluster level using sealed, sequentially numbered, opaque envelopes prepared by a sponsor agent independent of the trial team: 12 pairs, each containing one hypnosis and one relaxation allocation, yielding a 1:1 ratio across 24 clusters.
Envelopes were drawn immediately before each cohort began by a hospital representative independent of clinical care (S3).
Participants and practitioners were necessarily unmasked.
Outcome data collectors worked from datasets coded by envelope number, telephone interviewers were masked, and the trial statistician remained masked until the primary analyses were complete (S4).

All participants received the centre's standard 4-week residential PR programme: approximately 30 hours per week of cycle endurance training at 75% of peak work rate, strength training, COPD self-management workshops, dyspnoea-desensitisation workshops, and speech and singing therapy, plus needs-based psychological counselling and smoking-cessation support, identical in both arms (S5.1).
Participants in both arms also attended two 45-minute group sessions, on the Wednesdays of weeks 1 and 3.

Medical hypnosis sessions followed a standardised script comprising a hypnotic induction, suggestions of relaxation and of "air entering effortlessly into the lungs," nature-themed metaphors, and an explicit prescription to practice self-hypnosis for anxiety and dyspnoea throughout PR.

Structured relaxation sessions followed a standardised script of identical duration, structure, and prescription, comprising six dynamic relaxation exercises focused on proprioception, calmness, and breath regulation.
Scripts were not tailored (Appendices 3 and 4).

Both interventions were delivered by the same three practitioners (A.D., C.M., I.S.; Association Française d'Hypnose-certified, ≥4 years' experience), rotated by duty roster so that practitioner was fully crossed with allocation.

Fidelity rested on the verbatim scripts, practitioner certification and rotation, and a pass/fail delivery check performed once per cohort by the investigators leading clinical conduct (A.G. and B.H.; all passed); sessions were not recorded or rated at component level (S5.6).

The registration listed the STAI-6, HADS, and MDP as co-primary outcomes; analyses follow the published protocol (13), which designated the STAI-6 as primary and the others as additional robustness metrics, a redesignation made before any analysis (S8.2) which did not alter the results of the trial in any way.

text.text: The sample size was derived by simulation for a mixed-effects model with cluster random intercepts (13): 10 clusters of five participants per arm (n=100) gave 83% power (95% confidence interval, 80-86%) at a two-sided α of 0.05 to detect a 10% (approximately 4.7-point) additional STAI-6 reduction with hypnosis, assuming a 24% reduction with hypnosis, as in HYPNOBPCO_1 (9), and 14% with relaxation from a baseline of 47 points.
The target was set at 120 to allow for 20% attrition.
Given the novelty of the approach, no empirical pre-existing intracluster correlation coefficient was available at simulation time.
All analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all randomised participants except those who withdrew consent.
Because the programme was residential, the intention-to-treat and per-protocol sets were identical by design.

Missing items were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations (M = 100, item level) with predictive mean matching under a missing-at-random assumption; differential attrition at month 3 was addressed by a tipping-point sensitivity analysis (S8.3 and S8.11).

The primary analysis was a Bayesian analysis of covariance with a cluster-level random intercept, which adjusted for the baseline value of the outcome, baseline CAT, baseline 6-minute walk distance, age, and sex, fitted across the imputed datasets with weakly informative priors whose central 95% interval spanned several minimal clinically important differences (MCIDs) on each scale (S8.4).

For every outcome we report the posterior median between-arm contrast (hypnosis minus relaxation), its 95% highest-density interval (HDI), and the posterior probability that the contrast exceeded the MCID (STAI-6, 3 points, a precedent-based threshold in the absence of a COPD-specific MCID (S8.9); HADS-A, 1.5; MDP items, 1; MDP sums, 3; CAT, 2; 6-minute walk distance, 30 m).
The MDP thresholds are conservative and author-defined, as no validated MCID exists.
They are used descriptively only.
No Bayesian decision rule was prespecified; posterior probabilities are descriptive summaries, not success criteria.
The intracluster correlation coefficient was derived from the posterior variance components (21) (22) (23).

text.text: This approach replaced the registered constrained longitudinal model as the primary analysis to account for an unexpected baseline imbalance between arms, observed on arm-coded data before unmasking.
The registered model is retained nonetheless, as a secondary analysis (S8.5).
Of note, the change was found to be conservative with respect to the trial hypothesis.

Analysis of covariance conditions explicitly on each outcome's baseline value, and because the hypnosis arm entered the trial with lower anxiety, adjusting for baseline removes a head start that the registered model, which estimates each arm's trajectory from its observed starting point, would have credited to hypnosis (Results; S8.5).

A post hoc, exploratory moderation analysis, grounded in the sensory-affective structure of the MDP (16) and prior mechanistic work (9, 10), tested whether the hypnosis effect varied with baseline dyspnoea burden.

Two standardised composite indices were formed from preregistered week-1 values: a sensory-somatic index (mean z-score of the MDP-SQ sum and CAT) and an affective index (mean z-score of the MDP-A2 sum, HADS-A, and STAI-6), so that moderator and outcome roles were separated by time point (S7).

Bayesian analyses of covariance with continuous moderator-by-intervention interactions were fitted to the primary and confirmatory anxiety outcomes, and between-arm contrasts were reported at +1 SD on the sensory and -1 SD on the affective index, as an illustrative point on a continuum.
As part of this analytical strategy, HADS-A, which is not anchored to the respiratory experience, was designated post hoc as a within-construct negative control on which no gradient was expected.

For robustness, the moderation was also re-estimated with baseline STAI-6 and MDP-A2 sum removed from the index subsequently, so that no outcome moderated itself, and with the sensory index restricted to the MDP-SQ sum, removing the CAT's non-sensory items (Table 4).

text.text: No adverse events were reported and no deaths occurred in either arm.

No hypnosis-related event of interest (dissociative reaction, marked anxiety exacerbation, traumatic-memory reactivation, or distress from intrusive imagery requiring intervention) was recorded, and no participant discontinued rehabilitation because of either intervention (S10).

text.text: PR supplemented with mind-body adjunctive care showed clinically significant decreases in anxiety at programme's end.

The adjunctive medical hypnosis arm did not differ from the adjunctive structured relaxation arm: the population-level null was uniform across the primary and confirmatory anxiety outcomes, sensory dyspnoea, and functional capacity, while anxiety improved overall by more than the MCID (pooled change, -5.72 points; S8.13).
In the exploratory, post hoc moderation analysis, the hypnosis benefit on STAI-6 increased with baseline sensory burden and decreased with baseline affective burden.

The sensory pattern replicated across the confirmatory anxiety measures, was strongest on the MDP-A2 sum (0.985), was absent on HADS-A (i.e. the within-construct negative control) and held on the MDP-A2 sum, under every recomposition of the burden indices.
The STAI-6 gradient attenuated when recomputed without the CAT, reflecting a sensory-somatic composite rather than a purely sensory dyspnoea (Table 4).
text.formatted: The STAI-6 gradient attenuated when recomputed without the CAT, reflecting a sensory-somatic composite rather than a purely sensory dyspnoea (Table <ref type="table">4</ref>).

text.text: At the high-sensory, low-affective anchor, the predicted STAI-6 contrast was -9.26 points, close to three times the MCID.
These results thus hint at an intervention-specific benefit moderated by baseline dyspnoea profile, and pave the way to future trials stratified on burden as a relevant diagnostic variable.

Previous trials had shown an immediate anxiolytic effect of one hypnosis session in severe inpatient COPD (9), and hypnosis attenuating both dimensions of experimentally induced dyspnoea in healthy volunteers (10).

text.text: The present trial tested them in a cluster-randomised, active-comparator PR setting with Bayesian inference over multiply imputed data.

Unlike waitlist-or usual-care-controlled trials (8), holding the relaxation, motivation, and contact components constant (24) (25) (26) isolated the mechanism specific to hypnosis, sensory suggestion and interoceptive redirection (11, 27, 28).

text.text: The gradient analysis yielded a potential candidate responder profile: patients entering PR with high sensory and low affective dyspnoea burden may gain additional anxiety benefit from hypnosis, whereas those with high affective burden are predicted to be at least equally well served by relaxation.

This is consistent with the proposal that hypnotic interoceptive redirection engages cognitive-control and attentional resources that are less available under affective dysregulation, a process-level account grounded in prior work (12, 27, 29) that our design supports, and with evidence that sensory and affective improvements in breathlessness during PR track separate brain networks (30, 31).

text.text: Interestingly, the same affect-blunts-suggestion pattern has been found in gut-directed hypnotherapy for refractory irritable bowel syndrome, where higher symptom burden with lower anxiety predicted response (32), and in hypnotic analgesia, which outperforms relaxation on the sensory but not the affective dimension of chronic pain (33, 34).

text.text: For practice, the findings potentially support brief mind-body adjuncts to PR for patients with COPD and elevated anxiety, while cautioning against preferential adoption of hypnosis over relaxation for unselected patients.

Anxiety improved to a clinically meaningful degree in both arms, although, in the absence of a rehabilitation-only comparator, this within-arm change cannot be attributed to the adjunctive sessions specifically.

No adverse events attributable to either adjunct were recorded; both are deliverable by trained staff within existing PR resources and oriented to self-management, so continued benefit depends on uptake, modest here, which argues for structured adherence support.

In a multicentre study of 276 COPD outpatients, the affective dimension of dyspnoea was more pronounced in those with worse dyspnoea grade and symptom burden, pointing to the need of personalized treatment based on burden (35, 36).
text.formatted: In a multicentre study of 276 COPD outpatients, the affective dimension of dyspnoea was more pronounced in those with worse dyspnoea grade and symptom burden, pointing to the need of personalized treatment based on burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36)</ref>.

text.text: The present trial contributes to this outstanding need by presenting two different adjunctive interventions and their potential relevance for different dyspnoea profiles.

Unlike trait-based clusters derived from clinical characteristics and then examined for affective load (35), burden-profile phenotypes partition patients directly on the sensory-affective plane, making the targeted dimension the classifying variable.

We suggest a pragmatic next step would be a preregistered superiority trial that stratifies recruitment by baseline burden, allocates hypnosis and relaxation to the predicted candidate responder phenotypes, and tests the predicted contrast along STAI-6 MCIDs.
This trial has limitations.
First, the outcomes are patient-reported, so participants were necessarily unmasked.
Expectancy and credibility were balanced by randomisation and standardized via scripting, but they were not effectively measured.
No suggestibility scores were obtained at any stage either.

Second, despite extensive training on behalf of the practitioners, partial involuntary transfer of hypnotic communication cannot be excluded, given that these were live rather than tape-recorded interventions.
Third, the comparator was embedded in a programme already delivering interoceptive components to both arms.
Removing said components would have implied degrading the CHB current treatment standards, which was judged unacceptable.
The present contrast captures only the increment of sensory suggestion over relaxation.
Fourth, recruitment fell below target (pandemic-era reclassification, smaller cohorts).

Fifth, a single trial in a French residential centre has limited generalizability, and while fidelity was assured by design (verbatim scripts, a written conduct protocol, certified practitioners rotated across arms) and monitored by a pass/fail delivery check once per cohort, we acknowledge that we did not record the sessions to monitor adherence.
Sixth, the moderation was post hoc in operationalisation, not prospectively powered, and the cognitive processes invoked here are proposed interpretations based in the literature.
In a PR programme that improved anxiety overall, an adjunctive medical hypnosis arm did not reduce anxiety more than a matched structured relaxation arm.
The absence of a between-arm difference shows that in matched conditions the hypnotic component added nothing measurable for unselected patients.

However, by indexing each patient's sensory and affective dyspnoea burden with instruments already in routine use, this trial proposes, from an exploratory perspective, a testable candidate responder phenotype, and a framework for developing personalised, burden-based adjunctive therapy for anxiety in COPD. extension).
